newsitem.title: USA: Dismissed central banker represents Albania at IMF.
newsitem.headline: Dismissed central banker represents Albania at IMF.

text.p: The dismissed governor of Albania's central bank is representing his strife-torn country at the International Monetary Fund's spring meeting.
IMF officials said they had received no word from Tirana on the replacement of Kristaq Luniku as Bank of Albania governor and he therefore continued to be the official representative.
Albanian president Sali Berisha dismissed Luniku last week and appointed Qamil Tusha, deputy head of a state-run commercial bank, as his replacement.
Luniku told reporters he was in Washington working for his country at the IMF, but would prefer to go back to Tirana.
"I hope I'll be going back shortly to continue to work, not just as a governor, but in whatever position. I will never stop working for my country," Luniku said.
But he added: "I represent Albania (at the IMF). I don't want to create problems for the central bank."
Luniku, who left Albania two months ago, said he was not surprised at his dismisal by Berisha in view of the situation in Albania, where a financial scandal set off an armed uprising.
More than 300 people have died in the violence racking the impoverished Balkan country since the collapse of get-rich-quick pyramid investment schemes. Many weapons have been distributed.
"There is a criminal, political and credibility crisis," he said. He saw his dismisal from the central bank as an attempt to destroy one of the few independent institutions left in Albania.
"The central bank had been fighting very consistently against the pyramid investment schemes that had the support of politicians," he said.
The central bank had been trying to forestall a financial and banking collapse that inevitably developed into a serious social and political crisis, Luniku said.

The banished governor was sceptical that Albanian citizens would ever recover their investments from the failed pyramid schemes. Full compensation for the large number of victims would mean "very huge costs for the future of Albania."
"I don't know what the solution should be," he said.
